narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 59.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is more likely than passing, so the university treated your predicted risk as too high for admission. This is a probability, not a certainty. The decision did not use your gender or race; it was driven mainly by three academic factors. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and, in your case, pushed the prediction toward failure; at 3.30 it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, but the model still treated it as a risk signal. Your third-year class standing was the second most important factor and pushed toward passing—your decile of 9 was above the accepted average of 5.79. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and pushed toward failure; at 40 it was above the accepted average of 37.18, yet the model treated it as unfavorable. To respond, ask admissions for a formal review of your file, retake the LSAT if you can improve, and strengthen your academic record or bar-readiness evidence before reapplying. You may also ask whether provisional admission or an advising plan is possible.
